title: Breed Rankings
text:
The Breed Rank data gives information about different types of breek ranks. The specific dataset called breed_rank_all gives information about the ranking of each dog breed recorded from the years 2013 to 2020. There are 195 different types of breeds that this data set contains.
This data set is a Breed Rankings Dataset from Kkakey courtesy of American Kennel Club. This data has been made available by KKakey through the TidyTuesday Data Link

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

breed_rank_all <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2022/2022-02-01/breed_rank.csv')


ggplot(breed_rank_all, aes(x = `2013 Rank`, y = `2020 Rank`)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
    labs(title = "Dog Breed Rankings 2013 vs 2020" )








The graph compares the dog breed rankings from the year 2013 to the year 2020. The red slope line attemps to highlight how the ranking between each year doesn’t change much. It would be interesting to learn more about which specific breeds are farther away from this trendline.

title: Simpson Episodes
text:
This data set analyzes the episodes from the TV show The Simpsons. Episodes and script lines have been filtered to only include episodes from 2010 to 2016. The data contains information about the imdb rating, voting, number in the series, season, title, views, and more.
This dataset is a Simpsons Dataset from Kaggle which was made available to the public by Prashant Banerjee. Thank you to Nicolas Foss, Ed.D., MS with Iowa HHS who curated the data set in linked in TidyTuesday

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

simpsons_episodes <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-02-04/simpsons_episodes.csv')


ggplot(simpsons_episodes, aes(x = views, y = imdb_rating)) + 
    geom_point() +
    labs(title = "Rating vs Views of Simpsons Episodes" )








The graph compares the imdb rating to the views of each Simpson episode within the data set. While most of the data points are skewed to the right side, there are a handful of episodes that have 0 or close to 0 views, yet relatively good ratings. Overall, the greater the number of views, the greater the rating is.

title: The Office Quotes
text:
This data set has information on all of the lines spoken in the American sitcom show, The Office. The data set tracks all lines from all 9 seasons and includes the season, episode, line, character who spoke the line, and what number line it was in the entire show. In total there are 61,306 lines!
This dataset has been created by Kaggle and was originally scraped from a website called Office Quotes that is currently down.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

office_lines <- read.csv("the-office_lines.csv")



The code below gives you a ranking of each character, calculating the length of lines for each character from The Office. I calculated the length of each line for each character and the summed up the length of all of their lines.



Code
office_lines_changed <- office_lines |>
  group_by(Character) |>
  mutate(line_length = str_length(Line))|>
  summarize(total_length = sum(line_length, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(total_length)) |>
  head(10)




One of the most common phrases that is repeated in The Office is “That’s what she said.” The main character Michael often repeats this innapropriate joke and I wanted to count how many times this joke was repeated by each character. First I found it helpful to change each string to all lower case and then use a regular expression brackets to choose either a straight or curly apostrophe.



Code
office_lines |>
  mutate(Line = str_to_lower(Line))|>
  group_by(Character) |>
  summarize(exclaim_counter = sum(str_count(Line, "that['’]s what she said")))|>
  arrange(desc(exclaim_counter))

One of my favorite characters is Dwight Schrute. He is known as one of the most comedic characters in the show. Using lookarounds, I wrote code to see what the characters talk about when he is mentioned. Some examples are shown below.

  mutate(jim_string = (str_extract(Line, "(?<=Dwight )[^.?]+"))) |>
  na.omit() |>

The great love story of the sitcom is the story of Jim and Pam. In this code I used str_detect to count how many times they are mentioned together in a line.



Code
office_lines |>
  summarize(jam_count = sum(str_detect(Line, "Jim.+Pam"), na.rm = TRUE)) 


  jam_count
1       147





Code
office_lines_changed <- office_lines_changed |>
  mutate(Character = fct_lump(Character, n = 5, w = total_length))
  
office_lines_changed <- office_lines_changed |> 
  mutate(Character = fct_reorder(Character, total_length, .desc = TRUE))

ggplot(office_lines_changed, aes(x = Character, y = total_length, fill = Character))+
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    y = "Total Length of Lines",
    title = "Total Length of Lines of Characters in The Office"
  )










PLOT 1: Length of Lines of Characters in The Office If you wanted to see how big of a role each character has in The Office throughout all 9 seasons, one way to track this could be to calculate the length of their lines. This plot above calculates the total length of all of each characters lines in terms of the physical length of each word in their lines. From this plot we can see that Michael, the main character, speaks the most. I was surprised to see that Andy spoke more than Pam because I always thought Pam was one of the more prevelant characters in the show. The pink other column represents all of the other characters in the show who had smaller roles. Some of those characters include Kevin, Angela, Phyllis, and more.




Code
office_lines_dwight <- office_lines |>
  group_by(Season) |>
  summarize(dwight_string = sum(str_detect(Line, "Dwight"))) 

ggplot(office_lines_dwight, aes(x = Season, y = dwight_string, fill = Season))+
  geom_col()+
  labs(
    y = "'Dwight' Mentions",
    title = "How Often is 'Dwight' Mentioned in Each Season?"
  )










PLOT 2: How Often is Dwight Mentioned in Each Season?

Using concept of tracking the times Dwight is mentioned in the Office, I plotted how many times Dwight is mentioned in each season. This gives us insight to how often the other characters talk about Dwight each season. With this data we can see that generally over time his popularity in the show increases. Although in season 2 and 3 Dwight is mentioned a lot more than in Season 4, 6, and 7. It would be interested to compare the data of all of the other characters and see which seasons highlight individual plots for each character. Maybe Dwight is mentioned less in Season 4 because Jim and Pam start dating then and are mentioned more by other characters.
